questions.problem:
Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}\in V.$ Given that ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly dependent and ${{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent, which of the following statements are true?

- ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0$ has only zero solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0$
- ${v}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}$
- ${v}_{4}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent set, we obtain that

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

has a non-zero solution.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, solving equation ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0$ for ${v}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
{v}_{2}=-\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{x}_{3}}{{x}_{2}}{v}_{3}-\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{2}}{v}_{4}.
$$

Moreover, ${x}_{2}$ can't be zero because then

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

will have a non-zero solution and that's a contradiction as ${{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent.
Hence, ${v}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}.$

- Statement III is false. Since the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent set, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{3}+{x}_{3}{v}_{4}=0
$$

has no non-zero solution. Hence, ${v}_{4}$ is not a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}\in V.$ Given that ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly independent set and ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},\text{ }{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent one, which of the following statements are true?

- ${v}_{3}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{4}$
- ${v}_{4}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$
- ${v}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{4}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent set, we obtain that

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

has a non-zero solution. Moreover, ${x}_{3}$ can't be zero because then

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

will have a non-zero solution and that's a contradiction as ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent.
Therefore, from ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0,$ we get

$$
{v}_{3}=-\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{3}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{3}}{v}_{2}-\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{3}}{v}_{4}.
$$

This means that ${v}_{3}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{4}.$

- Statement II is false. Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly independent set, ${v}_{4}$ can not be a linear combination of other vectors.

- Statement III is false. Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly independent set, ${v}_{2}$ can not be a linear combination of other vectors.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the set of matrices ${A,B,C},$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

 
If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O,$ where $O$ is the $2\times 2$ zero-matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ not all zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{1} \\ -{x}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} & -{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} & 3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7{x}_{3} & {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} & 6{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+7{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} & 3{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+7{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are  the $1$st and $2$nd. Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 

The system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+7{x}_{3}=0 \\ -3{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the $2$nd equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2{x}_{3}.$ Substitute it into the the first equation to get 

$$
{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}+7{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-3{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is
$[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.$

Finally, for any ${x}_{3}\ne 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=\frac{-3{x}_{3}}{-2{x}_{3}}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the set ${{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ of polynomials from $R[t],$ where

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1-3t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=-3+9t.
$$

If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}\cdot {p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}\cdot {p}_{2}(t)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ not both zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(1-3t)+{x}_{2}(-3+9t) & =0 \\ ({x}_{1}-3{x}_{2})+(-3{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2})t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
{\begin{aligned}1{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot column is the $1$st one. Hence, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the $1$st equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, for any ${x}_{2}\ne 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3{x}_{2}}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the set of matrices ${A,B,C},$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 3 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 
If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{3}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O,$ where $O$ is the $2\times 2$ zero-matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ not all zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-8 & 3 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 0 \\ -{x}_{1} & -{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-8{x}_{2} & 3{x}_{2} \\ -5{x}_{2} & 4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}10{x}_{3} & -3{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} & -5{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+10{x}_{3} & 3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} & -{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+10{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -8 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}/2 \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd. Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 

The system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the $2$nd equation, we get ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substitute it into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}+5{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is
$[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.$

Finally, for any ${x}_{3}\ne 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{3}}=\frac{{x}_{3}}{{x}_{3}}=1.
$$
